items.title: Frank Chace Interview, 1961-11-18
items.q: I was wondering if Omer Simeon wasn't a more important influence on the younger white Chicago players... Somehow I do, and I don't know why, really.

ctx.x: He wasn't usually the soloist on early records, was he? The peppers you talk about might have been the first time that he appeared as a soloist.

For all I know. His ensemble work is excellent. Of course, there's another manner of approach to the style, the method of playing ensemble. Now, they tell me that Jelly wrote out all the parts of the red hot peppers. I don't believe it. It's impossible. But Simeon would move around in the ensembles in a way that kind of forecasts the hot style of playing.

Before we leave Noon entirely, I want to mention that several people were influenced into succeeding generations by Noon, according to their own testimony. Johnny Lane has spoken about Noon as being, in his mind, the model clarinet player. And if I remember correctly, Lane taught Joe Marsala.
